questions.q: A single region at 99.9% uptime has about 525.6 minutes of annual downtime. Why does running two INDEPENDENT regions in active-active configuration reduce that to about 0.526 minutes?
options: The combined system only fails if BOTH regions fail at the same time, and the probability of two independent failures coinciding is much lower than either failing alone
Running two regions always doubles the downtime instead of reducing it
Two regions can never both be down according to this formula regardless of circumstances
The calculation only works if the two regions are located on the same continent
questions.explain: Combined failure probability for independent events is the PRODUCT of their individual failure probabilities, which is why 0.1% x 0.1% becomes a much smaller combined failure rate -- as long as the failures are genuinely independent.

questions.q: What is the critical assumption behind the two-region availability math, and what breaks it?
options: The assumption that the two regions' failures are independent -- a shared dependency (same model API provider, same auth service, same cloud billing account) can take both regions down simultaneously, silently invalidating the math
The assumption that both regions are staffed by the same engineering team
The assumption that both regions use the exact same programming language
There is no real assumption -- the math holds under all circumstances
questions.explain: The redundancy math only holds if the two regions can't fail for the same underlying reason -- any shared dependency between them reintroduces a single point of failure that the math doesn't account for.

questions.q: What is a failure mode specific to AI systems that a traditional database-backed web application does NOT have to plan for?
options: A third-party model API provider having an outage, hitting a rate limit, or silently degrading answer quality after a model update
The database running out of disk space
A server crashing due to a hardware failure
A network partition between two data centers
questions.explain: Database outages, server crashes, and network partitions are failure modes any production system has to handle; depending on an external model API introduces failure modes (provider outage, rate limiting, silent quality drift) that are specific to AI systems.

questions.q: Why is 'silent quality degradation' described as arguably the hardest of the three AI-specific failure modes to detect?
options: The API keeps returning successful (200 OK) responses even as answer quality quietly drops, so nothing obviously LOOKS broken -- it requires dedicated drift/quality monitoring to catch, not just uptime checks
Silent quality degradation always triggers an immediate, obvious error message
This failure mode is actually the easiest of the three to detect using standard uptime monitoring
Silent quality degradation never actually occurs in real production AI systems
questions.explain: Unlike an outage or a rate-limit error, nothing in the response itself signals a problem -- the system appears healthy by every standard uptime metric while quietly serving worse answers, which is why dedicated drift detection (not uptime monitoring) is the actual fix.

questions.q: What is graceful degradation, and why does it require real design work in advance?
options: A planned, reduced-functionality fallback mode (e.g., showing raw retrieved documents instead of an LLM-generated summary) that must be deliberately designed, since a system with no defined degraded mode just fails completely when its primary path breaks
A feature that automatically and perfectly repairs any failure with no engineering effort required
A synonym for simply shutting the entire system down during any failure
A failure mode that only affects multi-region systems, never single-region ones
questions.explain: Graceful degradation is a deliberate fallback that has to be designed and built ahead of time -- without one, a broken primary path means the whole system goes down instead of serving a reduced but functioning experience.
